name: Ramalama Costume Walk
peak: Peaking now (mid to late Oct 2026), runs to 31 Oct
timeline: First seen 29 Jul 2025 and peaked around Halloween 2025 (one Oct 2025 video reached about 94M views). Revived from Aug 2026. Listed at the Peak stage with 456K videos in the third week of Oct 2026.
what: A low camera on the creator's feet as they stalk slowly towards the lens, then a hard cut on the beat reveals the full costume.
format: Low-angle walk-up, one cut, full reveal
why_now: It's the default costume-reveal sound for Halloween 2026. New Engen ranks it the #2 TikTok trend of October.
brand_use: Swap the costume for a product, a mascot or a staff member in uniform. The slow walk-up builds suspense for any reveal, so it also works for a new menu item, a store fit-out or a packaging redesign.
example_brief: A sneaker retailer films only the new shoe stalking down the aisle, then cuts to the full outfit on the drop.
risk: Halloween is smaller in Australia, so lean on the 'big reveal' rather than the spooky angle. Check the track is cleared in the commercial music library before posting from a brand account.

name: Two Fishes
peak: Peaking in Oct 2026 (New Engen's audio of the month)
timeline: The clip comes from Love Island USA Season 8 and was circulating by early Jul 2026. It took off again as a 'confidently wrong' lip-sync in Oct 2026 and spun off into Halloween costumes by 10 Oct.
what: Creators lip-sync the Love Island 'two fish' speech to defend a questionable opinion with total conviction.
sound: Love Island USA 'two fish' audio (credited to Sincere in most posts)
why_now: The 'confidently wrong' tone gets people arguing in the comments, which pushes reach.
brand_use: Have the brand defend a harmless, slightly unhinged opinion about its own category, e.g. 'pineapple belongs on pizza'. It builds personality and comments without any product push.
example_brief: A pizza chain's social lead lip-syncs it to defend pineapple, with the menu item in shot.
risk: Reality-TV audio, so check the clearance. Sources disagree on which islander is speaking, so don't name them in captions.

name: Text message from -A
peak: Peaked 23 Sep to early Oct 2026, still in mid-Oct round-ups
timeline: Wave started 19 Sep 2026. Shay Mitchell joined on 23 Sep and Lucy Hale opened her TikTok with it on 24 Sep. One post had 8.7M views by 29 Sep. Later, Ramdam and SocialBee were still listing it on 2, 5 and 14 Oct.
what: An on-screen 'text' signed '-A', Pretty Little Liars style, calls out a specific habit. Then the creator is caught doing exactly that.
format: Fake text overlay, then a caught-in-the-act clip
why_now: 2016 nostalgia is running hot and the cast joined in. The format slots into any niche.
brand_use: '-A' exposes the brand's fans: 'I know you added three more to cart at 1am. -A'. It also suits apps, as an exposé of a shortcut that users love.
example_brief: A food-delivery client's '-A' texts call out the person ordering 'just a drink' and getting dessert as well.
risk: It's past peak, so post this week or skip it.

name: Getting robbed
peak: Peaking early to mid Oct 2026
timeline: The original sound went up 26 Apr 2026 and brands like Vice Versa used it in Aug. Later listed it for Reels on 2 Oct and for TikTok on 16 Oct 2026.
what: A one-shot skit: someone is so absorbed in their phone that their bag gets stolen right behind them. The caption says what they were too distracted by.
format: Single locked-off shot with a text overlay
why_now: One take, no editing, any niche. Later flagged it as the easiest trend of mid-October.
brand_use: Make the brand's content the distraction: 'me getting robbed because the new episode dropped'. It works for streaming, publishing, gaming, retail drops and sports.
example_brief: A streaming client: a viewer glued to the season finale doesn't notice their bag, couch and dog leave the room.
risk: Keep the theft obviously staged and comedic so it doesn't read as real crime footage.

name: My reaction
peak: Rising now (from 29 Sep 2026), likely peaking late Oct
timeline: The sound was posted 29 Sep 2026. Brands joined in Oct: Minki Haircare on 2 Oct and Polizei Österreich (Austrian police) on 15 Oct. Later listed it on 16 Oct.
what: Rank or judge something from your niche using only facial expressions. Your face is the scoring system.
format: Text prompt plus a reaction-face close-up
why_now: It's early in its cycle and brands are already doing well with it. It also starts arguments in the comments.
brand_use: The social lead reacts to customer habits, competitor clichés or product hacks. It's cheap to make, quick to post and very on-brand for anything with a fandom.
example_brief: A coffee client's barista reacts to drink orders: 'extra hot oat latte' gets a slow, pained blink.

name: October is all about me
peak: Seasonal: peaks 1 to 31 Oct 2026
timeline: The Drake line is from 2023's 'Slime You Out' and comes back every October. This year's version of the sound was posted 21 Sep 2026 and Later called it 'all over the FYP' on 16 Oct.
what: The 'October is all about me' line over a simple clip and on-screen text: main-character, birthday-month energy.
format: One clip plus a text overlay
why_now: It's the anthem for the month and it expires on 1 November.
brand_use: Use it for October launches, October birthdays, or a brand that owns the month (Halloween ranges, spring racing, footy finals wrap-ups). It's a quick 'our month' flex.
example_brief: A fashion client posts its October drop with 'October is all about me' over a slow-mo try-on.
risk: Only good until 31 Oct. It's Drake audio, so check commercial clearance.

name: I just want to be OK
peak: Peaking late Sep to mid Oct 2026
timeline: Picked up through Aug and Sep 2026 on Ingrid Michaelson's 'Be OK'. Later listed it on 2 Oct, and New Engen and SocialBee had it in their mid-Oct round-ups (14 Oct).
what: Creators dance or potter around happily while the caption reveals the stress they're ignoring.
format: Upbeat clip plus a 'secretly stressed' caption
why_now: Relatable 'quietly falling apart' humour is landing well as people head into end-of-year burnout.
brand_use: Caption the stress your customer has and let the product be the reason they really are OK. It suits finance, insurance, telcos, travel and wellness.
example_brief: An insurance client: someone dancing through the kitchen, captioned 'me pretending the hail damage isn't real', then 'actually covered'.
risk: Keep it light. The phrase is also used for sincere mental-health posts, so avoid anything that mocks real distress.

name: The 'Oh look' trend
peak: Peaked Sep to early Oct 2026
timeline: The sound dates from Mar 2025. It was revived in early Sep 2026, Ramdam listed it on 5 Oct, and SocialBee still had it on 14 Oct.
what: Two people: one points something out, the other panics dramatically, then the reveal flips to a calm, simple fix (or a funnier, more personal fear).
why_now: It's a ready-made problem/solution structure, which is why Ramdam called it out for apps and services.
brand_use: Panic over the manual, annoying version of a task, then calm when someone produces the brand's product. It's ideal for B2B, apps, logistics and admin-heavy services.
example_brief: A logistics client: a business owner panics over a lost parcel, then goes calm when the colleague opens the tracking app.

name: Pumpkin Head Illusion
peak: Rising now, should peak in the last week of Oct 2026
timeline: New Engen's October round-up (updated 14 Oct) lists it as a Halloween pick. New posts were still coming on 17 and 19 Oct 2026.
what: A forced-perspective shot makes a pumpkin look like it has replaced a friend's head while they dance.
why_now: It's the visual Halloween trick of the season and it's still climbing.
brand_use: Replace the head with the product: a burger, a candle, a perfume bottle. It's a playful product hero shot that takes just one camera trick.
example_brief: A candle brand lines up its pumpkin-spice candle as the dancer's head, then flicks it alight on the beat.
risk: Halloween-specific and less relevant in Australia. Product-swap versions work all year round.

name: Fan Transition
peak: Peaking early to mid Oct 2026
timeline: The Tab covered it on 28 Sep 2026, and Later listed it for Reels on 9 Oct. SocialPilot had the 'Girls on Film' sound Rising for 12 to 25 Oct, and new posts were landing on 6 and 7 Oct.
what: Shot from overhead lying under a ceiling fan. Each blade pass wipes to a new outfit.
why_now: It's the transition of the month, and AI templates make it easy, so it's everywhere.
brand_use: Fashion, beauty and retail: a range or a 'week of looks' in one blade-wipe sequence. It also suits paint, bedding or homewares, if you swap outfits for room makeovers.
example_brief: A department store client runs five spring looks in one fan spin, ending on the price card.
risk: 'Girls on Film' is a major-label track and restricted for business accounts, so use a cleared sound. Many viral versions are AI-generated. If the client's version is AI, say so.

name: Netflix Documentary
peak: First peak Jul 2026 (TikTok), second wave on Instagram in Oct 2026
timeline: Started on TikTok on 16 Jun 2026. A 30 Jun video drew 11.5M views in two weeks, and brands like Dynamite Clothing jumped on in Jul. Anijam reported in Oct that it had crossed over and was trending on its own on Instagram.
what: Sat in a chair under moody light with a documentary score, the creator narrates something mundane as if it were a true-crime confession.
why_now: Instagram is running its own second wave, and it's one of the most brand-friendly formats of the year.
brand_use: Turn the brand's origin story or a tiny product detail into a solemn documentary. It's great for founders, craft brands and anyone with a quirky backstory.
example_brief: A bakery owner, lit like a true-crime subject: 'It was 4am. The sourdough had not risen. We had 200 pre-orders.'
risk: Don't use Netflix branding, logos or the 'N' sound. Keep the parody generic.

name: Things you should definitely ghost
peak: Peaks the last two weeks of Oct (it did in 2025 and is back for 2026)
timeline: Brands like Curology used it for Halloween 2025. Australian candle retailer Dusk brought it back in Sep 2026, and Oct 2026 posts include salons and clinics (3 and 8 Oct).
what: Someone in a bedsheet ghost costume holds up signs listing bad habits in their industry to 'ghost', ending on the better way.
why_now: It's a Halloween format that doubles as useful advice, so it gets saved and shared.
brand_use: It turns category myths into a list of things to 'ghost'. Service brands own this one: banks, salons, clinics, gyms, SaaS.
example_brief: A banking client's ghost holds up signs: 'hidden fees', 'manual transfers', 'waiting on hold'.

name: Daily GRWM loading
peak: Rising since 2 Oct 2026, still climbing
timeline: Later listed it for Reels on 2 Oct 2026. TikTok versions followed on 8 and 16 Oct, and SocialPilot has the sound Rising for 12 to 25 Oct.
what: A get-ready-with-me that starts at '0%' in pyjamas and loads up with each cut until the finished look at 100%.
why_now: The loading bar keeps people watching to 100%, which is exactly what the algorithm rewards.
brand_use: Anything with a build-up can use the loading bar: a dish being plated, a car being detailed, a room being styled, a team getting ready for an event.
example_brief: A restaurant client 'loads' a signature dish from 0% raw ingredients to 100% on the pass.

name: "Let's…"
peak: New this week (listed 14 Oct 2026)
timeline: SocialBee added it as its newest Instagram trend on 14 Oct 2026.
what: The creator shrugs off a run of invitations without reacting, then switches to a hyped edit for the one thing they actually love.
format: Deadpan cuts, then a high-energy edit
why_now: It's brand new this week, so early movers get the reach.
brand_use: 'Let's go for a run?' gets nothing. 'Let's get [brand]?' gets the hype edit. It's a simple way to make the product the one thing worth getting excited about.
example_brief: A gelato client: no reaction to gym, early nights or meal prep, then full-energy cuts for 'let's get gelato'.

name: "Yes… but"
peak: Rising since 7 Oct 2026
timeline: SocialBee listed it on 7 Oct 2026, and it's still in their 14 Oct update.
what: A split screen: the appealing side ('yes') next to its honest downside ('but').
why_now: Honest, self-aware brand content is beating polished ads, and this format is built for it.
brand_use: Brands poke fun at themselves: 'Yes, our burger is huge. But you will need a nap.' It works well for hospitality, travel and fitness.
example_brief: A travel client: 'Yes, Bali for $499' next to 'but your boss will see the tan'.

name: Money can't buy happiness, but…
peak: Peaking Sep to Oct 2026
timeline: SocialPilot's archive has the sound from Sep 2026. Later re-listed it for Reels on 16 Oct, and brands like Arabella Jewelry were still posting it on 19 Oct.
what: 'Money can't buy happiness, but it can buy…', followed by a quick clip of the thing that obviously brings joy.
why_now: It's one of the most direct sell formats around, and audiences still accept it.
brand_use: It's essentially a product shot with a punchline, suited to retail, food, beauty and experiences. Put the hero product or a customer's reaction at the reveal.
example_brief: A jewellery client: 'Money can't buy happiness, but it can buy this', then the ring box opens.
risk: It reads as an ad, so keep the reveal genuinely delightful.

name: Pray For Me slow-mo entrance
peak: Rising in Oct 2026
timeline: Listed in New Engen's October 2026 round-up (updated 14 Oct).
what: Friends take turns making exaggerated slow-motion entrances into ordinary places (the office, the supermarket, the school pick-up).
sound: Pray For Me, The Weeknd and Kendrick Lamar
why_now: It's a group format, so it's good for team culture content at a time when that's doing well.
brand_use: The staff make hero entrances into the store, kitchen or office. It humanises the brand and suits launch days or end-of-year team content.
example_brief: A hotel's housekeeping team walks the corridor in slow-mo, then reveals a perfect room.
risk: Major-label track, so use a cleared alternative on brand accounts if it's restricted.

name: we fell in love in october
peak: Peak stage now (Oct 2026), as every October
timeline: The girl in red song comes back every October. SocialPilot has it at the Peak stage for 12 to 25 Oct 2026, with about 2M TikTok videos and 1M Reels, and it's on the MusicMaestro US chart for week 40.
what: Soft, nostalgic montages: coffee pours, scarves, slow afternoons, couples, cosy interiors.
sound: we fell in love in october, girl in red
why_now: It's the most-used seasonal sound of the month on both platforms.
brand_use: Hospitality, florists, homewares and couples photographers can do an easy mood piece. For Australia, flip it to spring: picnics, jacarandas, first swims.
example_brief: A Sydney café client: jacaranda petals, an iced latte and the first warm evening, set to the sound.
risk: The autumn imagery is northern hemisphere and it's spring in Australia, so localise it.

name: Goo Goo Muck: 'my decoration is alive'
peak: Peak stage now, through 31 Oct 2026
timeline: The Cramps track comes back every Halloween (it's been huge since Netflix's Wednesday). SocialPilot has it at the Peak stage with about 305K Reels for 12 to 25 Oct 2026.
what: A Halloween prop, or a person posing as one, moves perfectly on the beat as if it has come alive.
why_now: It's the Halloween comedy sound of the week on Reels.
brand_use: Bring the store mascot, a mannequin or a window display to life. It's good for retail, bars and attractions with a Halloween activation.
example_brief: A department store's window mannequin twitches into the dance as shoppers walk past.
risk: It's restricted for business accounts (major label), so do it with a creator partner or a cleared sound-alike.

name: The Process (behind the scenes)
peak: Steady since 18 Sep 2026, a business-friendly staple
timeline: Later listed it on 18 Sep 2026, and SocialPilot's October archive still has it among the trending business sounds.
what: A step-by-step walk through the tools, materials and effort behind a product or service, ending on the finished result.
why_now: Craft and transparency content is beating polished ads, and it's original audio, so it's safe for business accounts.
brand_use: Show the making of anything: a campaign shoot, a hand-finished product, a fit-out, a dish. It suits agencies' own channels as well as clients'.
example_brief: Apparent's own channel: from brief to shoot to final frame of a recent campaign, set to 'The Process'.
